document.title: Toronto Notes 2025
document.subtitle: Comprehensive Medical Reference and Review for the MCCQE, 41st edition

questions.question: A 68-year-old man is assessed in the preoperative clinic before an open cholecystectomy. He has unstable coronary artery disease with angina at rest and symptomatic congestive heart failure requiring recent hospitalization. He is not moribund and is expected to survive well beyond 24 hours. Which of the following American Society of Anesthesiologists physical status classifications best describes him?
questions.explanation: The ASA classification describes physical status at the time of surgery. ASA 4 is a patient with severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life, with unstable coronary artery disease and symptomatic congestive heart failure given as examples. ASA 3 describes severe systemic disease limiting activity, such as stable CAD, and ASA 5 is a moribund patient not expected to survive 24 hours without surgery.

optionExplanations.a: ASA 1 describes a healthy, fit patient.
optionExplanations.b: ASA 2 describes mild systemic disease such as controlled type 2 diabetes, controlled hypertension, obesity or smoking.
optionExplanations.c: ASA 3 describes severe systemic disease limiting activity, for example stable CAD, COPD or poorly controlled diabetes.
optionExplanations.e: ASA 5 is reserved for a moribund patient not expected to survive 24 hours without the operation, such as ruptured AAA.

source.reference: A4 — American Society of Anesthesiology Classification

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman with no significant comorbidities is scheduled for an elective laparoscopic procedure. She asks the anesthesiologist how long before the operation she must stop drinking water and pulp-free apple juice. She has no condition that delays gastric emptying. According to the Canadian Anesthesiologists' Society fasting guidelines, what is the minimum fasting interval for clear fluids in an adult before an elective procedure?
questions.explanation: Before elective procedures the minimum fasting duration for clear fluids in adults, including water, pulp-free juice, complex carbohydrate beverages and tea or coffee without milk, is 2 hours. Solids and non-human milk or fortified expressed breast milk require 6 hours, breast milk 4 hours, and clear fluids in infants and children 1 hour.

optionExplanations.a: One hour is the minimum for clear fluid intake in infants and children, not adults.
optionExplanations.c: Four hours applies to ingestion of breast milk.
optionExplanations.d: Six hours applies to solid meals, infant formula, non-human milk or fortified expressed breast milk.
optionExplanations.e: Eight hours exceeds the recommended interval and unnecessarily prolongs fasting.

source.reference: A5 — Fasting Guidelines Prior to Surgery

questions.question: A 66-year-old man is referred for elective inguinal hernia repair. Three weeks ago he had a myocardial infarction managed medically without coronary intervention. He is currently asymptomatic on optimal medical therapy, and the hernia is reducible and not causing obstructive symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Postpone the operation until at least 60 days have elapsed since the myocardial infarction
Proceed with the operation now under general anesthesia
Proceed with the operation now under spinal anesthesia
Postpone the operation for one week and then proceed
Proceed now with postoperative ICU monitoring

questions.explanation: ACC/AHA guidelines recommend that at least 60 days elapse after a myocardial infarction before non-cardiac surgery in the absence of a coronary intervention, because this period carries an increased risk of re-infarction and death, and mortality with perioperative MI is 20-50%. Since this hernia repair is elective and can be delayed, the surgery should be deferred.

optionExplanations.b: Operating within the high-risk window after myocardial infarction increases re-infarction and death for an elective case that can wait.
optionExplanations.c: Choosing a different anesthetic technique does not remove the elevated risk associated with recent infarction.
optionExplanations.d: One week falls far short of the recommended 60-day interval.
optionExplanations.e: Invasive intra- and postoperative ICU monitoring is the strategy when a procedure is essential and cannot be delayed, which is not the case here.

questions.question: A 38-year-old woman requires an emergency appendectomy. She ate a full meal one hour before the onset of pain, has longstanding gastroesophageal reflux disease with a hiatus hernia, and has received parenteral opioid analgesia in the emergency department. Her airway examination is reassuring. Which of the following is the most appropriate airway plan for induction of general anesthesia?

options.text: Inhalational induction with a laryngeal mask airway
Routine IV induction with bag-mask ventilation followed by intubation
Rapid sequence induction with cricoid pressure and a cuffed endotracheal tube
Supraglottic airway with maintained spontaneous ventilation
Deep sedation with a simple face mask

questions.explanation: This patient has multiple aspiration risk factors: inadequate fasting, delayed gastric emptying from narcotics, decreased sphincter competence from GERD and hiatus hernia, and an acute abdomen. Management is to use a protected airway with an endotracheal tube, reduce gastric volume and acidity, and employ rapid sequence induction, in which bag-mask ventilation is avoided and cricoid pressure may be applied.

optionExplanations.a: A laryngeal mask or any supraglottic device leaves the airway unprotected and is itself listed as an aspiration risk factor.
optionExplanations.b: Bag-mask ventilation is avoided in rapid sequence induction because it can increase the risk of aspiration.
optionExplanations.d: Spontaneous ventilation through a supraglottic airway does not protect against regurgitation of gastric contents.
optionExplanations.e: Deep sedation with an unprotected airway reduces the level of consciousness and increases aspiration risk.

questions.topic: Aspiration Risk and Rapid Sequence Induction

questions.question: A 27-year-old man requires emergency laparotomy after a stabbing. He is hypovolemic from ongoing hemorrhage, with blood pressure 84/48 mmHg and heart rate 128 bpm despite resuscitation. He is being taken directly to the operating room and requires immediate induction of general anesthesia. Which of the following induction agents is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Ketamine is a dissociative agent that increases heart rate, blood pressure, systemic vascular resistance and coronary flow, and it is indicated for induction when sympathetic stimulation is required, such as major trauma and hypovolemia. It is also used for IM induction in children or uncooperative adults and in severe asthma because of its sympathomimetic and bronchodilating effects.

optionExplanations.a: Propofol decreases systemic vascular resistance, blood pressure and stroke volume, and should be used with caution in patients who cannot tolerate a sudden fall in blood pressure.
optionExplanations.c: Thiopental decreases cardiac output and blood pressure and is cautioned against in uncontrolled hypotension, shock and cardiac failure.
optionExplanations.d: Etomidate is indicated for poor cardiac function and severe valve lesions rather than as the agent of choice for hemorrhagic hypovolemia, and it causes adrenal suppression after a single dose.
optionExplanations.e: Midazolam is described as a sedation agent rather than one of the listed intravenous induction agents for this scenario.

questions.question: An anesthesiologist is planning maintenance with sevoflurane for two patients undergoing the same operation: a fit 30-year-old and a fit 80-year-old. Both are normothermic, have received no premedication, and have no history of substance use. The anesthesiologist expects the required minimum alveolar concentration to differ between them. Which of the following factors decreases the minimum alveolar concentration requirement?
questions.explanation: MAC is the minimum alveolar concentration of a volatile anesthetic that prevents movement in 50% of patients in response to a surgical stimulus, and it is the measure used to compare potency. MAC of halogenated volatile anesthetics decreases by approximately 6% per additional decade of age in adults, so the older patient requires a lower concentration.

optionExplanations.b: Chronic alcohol use is listed among the factors that increase MAC.
optionExplanations.c: Hyperthermia increases MAC, whereas hypothermia decreases it.
optionExplanations.d: Acute amphetamine use increases MAC, while chronic amphetamine use decreases it.
optionExplanations.e: Hyperthyroidism is listed among the factors that increase MAC.

questions.question: A 30-year-old man sustained third-degree burns to 40% of his body surface area five days ago. He now requires general anesthesia with rapid airway control for wound debridement, and he is at risk of regurgitation because of a recently fed nasogastric tube. His airway examination is normal. Which of the following neuromuscular blocking agents is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Succinylcholine can cause massive potassium release through proliferation of extrajunctional cholinergic receptors, and patients with third-degree burns from 24 hours to 6 months after injury are at high risk for a hyperkalemic response, an absolute contraindication. High-dose rocuronium has a quick onset that allows its use in rapid sequence induction and is the appropriate alternative.

optionExplanations.a: Succinylcholine is contraindicated in patients at high risk of hyperkalemic response, including third-degree burns 24 hours to 6 months after injury.
optionExplanations.c: Vecuronium has an onset of 2-3 minutes, which is too slow for rapid airway control.
optionExplanations.d: Cisatracurium also has an onset of about 2-3 minutes and is not suited to rapid sequence induction.
optionExplanations.e: Pancuronium is long acting with a 3-5 minute onset and causes tachycardia.

source.reference: A19 — Depolarizing and Non-Depolarizing Muscle Relaxants

questions.question: A 19-year-old man under general anesthesia with sevoflurane, who received succinylcholine at induction, develops an unexplained rise in end-tidal CO2, tachycardia, generalized muscle rigidity and diaphoresis 30 minutes into the case. Core temperature is climbing. The surgeon has been notified, triggering agents have been discontinued, charcoal filters inserted, and he is hyperventilated with 100% oxygen. Which of the following is the most appropriate next treatment?
questions.explanation: This is malignant hyperthermia, a hypermetabolic disorder of skeletal muscle triggered by all inhalational agents except nitrous oxide and by succinylcholine, presenting with rising end-tidal CO2, tachycardia, rigidity and late hyperthermia. After notifying the surgeon, stopping triggers and hyperventilating with 100% oxygen, dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg IV through a large-bore IV is given and repeated until the signs are controlled.

optionExplanations.b: Sodium bicarbonate is given for a base excess worse than -8 on blood gas, or as part of hyperkalemia treatment, after dantrolene.
optionExplanations.c: Calcium chloride is used for life-threatening hyperkalemia complicating malignant hyperthermia rather than as the primary treatment.
optionExplanations.d: Glucose with insulin is a component of hyperkalemia management, not the specific antidote for the hypermetabolic crisis.
optionExplanations.e: Furosemide is considered for maintaining fluid output later in management and does not treat the underlying disorder.

questions.question: A 58-year-old man is brought to the operating room for an emergency laparotomy for a perforated viscus. His level of consciousness is decreased and gastric contents are visible in his oropharynx. The team is ventilating him by bag and mask with a jaw thrust while equipment is prepared. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to support his airway?

options.text: Continue bag and mask ventilation with a chin lift
Insert an oropharyngeal airway and continue bag and mask ventilation

questions.explanation: Methods of supporting the airway are divided into non-definitive airways, which are patent only (jaw thrust or chin lift, oropharyngeal and nasopharyngeal airways, bag mask ventilation, and the LMA), and definitive airways, which are patent and protected (an endotracheal tube or a surgical airway). Indications for intubation include a patent airway, protection against aspiration, positive pressure ventilation, pulmonary toilet, and pharmacologic administration. With a decreased level of consciousness and gastric contents present, only a cuffed endotracheal tube protects this airway.

optionExplanations.a: Bag and mask ventilation carries a risk of aspiration when the level of consciousness is decreased or gastric contents are present, and it cannot ensure airway patency.
optionExplanations.b: An oropharyngeal airway only facilitates patency during bag and mask ventilation and offers no protection against aspiration.
optionExplanations.c: A nasopharyngeal airway is also a non-definitive airway that leaves the airway unprotected.
optionExplanations.d: An LMA is easy to insert but carries a risk of gastric aspiration and does not protect against laryngospasm or gastric aspiration.

questions.question: A 61-year-old woman undergoes induction of general anesthesia for elective surgery. Two attempts at laryngoscopy fail to pass the endotracheal tube through the cords. Help has been called. Bag and mask ventilation with 100% oxygen remains inadequate after an oral airway is inserted, and her oxygen saturation is falling. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Make a third attempt at direct laryngoscopy with the same blade
Attempt ventilation with a laryngeal mask airway
Proceed to a percutaneous surgical airway

questions.explanation: When intubation is unsuccessful after induction, the priority is to call for help and ventilate with 100% oxygen by bag and mask, since oxygenation and ventilation take priority over intubation. If bag and mask ventilation is inadequate, the sequence is to call for help, attempt ventilation with an oral airway, then consider or attempt an LMA, and only then emergency invasive airway access. An oral airway has already failed here, so an LMA is the next step.

optionExplanations.a: Failed attempts at intubation make further attempts more difficult because of tissue trauma, and ventilation must be re-established first.
optionExplanations.c: Emergency invasive airway access is reserved for after an oral airway and an LMA have failed to restore ventilation.
optionExplanations.d: Jet ventilation is listed among emergency invasive airway access options, which come after an attempt with an LMA.
optionExplanations.e: Retrograde intubation is also an emergency invasive access technique and is not the next step while a supraglottic option remains untried.

questions.question: A 26-year-old man is extubated while still semi-conscious at the end of an elective knee arthroscopy. He immediately develops stridor that progresses to no air movement, and his oxygen saturation falls to 84%. The pharynx has been suctioned, the oral airway removed, and CPAP with 100% oxygen using the anesthetic reservoir bag plus a low dose of propofol have failed to relieve the obstruction. Which of the following is the most appropriate next treatment?
questions.explanation: Laryngospasm is a forceful involuntary spasm of the laryngeal muscles caused by stimulation of the superior laryngeal nerve by oropharyngeal secretions, blood, or early extubation, and it causes partial or total airway obstruction, most often in semi-conscious patients. Treatment is suction, removal of the oral airway or LMA, CPAP with the anesthetic reservoir bag and partial closure of the adjustable pressure-limiting valve, bag mask ventilation with 100% oxygen, optional low-dose propofol 0.5-1.0 mg/kg, and then low-dose succinylcholine of approximately 0.25 mg/kg, with re-intubation if hypoxia develops.

optionExplanations.b: A full intubating dose of a non-depolarizing relaxant is not the described treatment for laryngospasm, which uses a low dose of succinylcholine.
optionExplanations.c: Nebulized bronchodilator therapy targets bronchospasm rather than spasm of the laryngeal muscles.
optionExplanations.d: A steroid does not act quickly enough to relieve an acute total airway obstruction from laryngospasm.
optionExplanations.e: Neostigmine is a reversal agent for non-depolarizing relaxants and does not break laryngospasm.

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman received a spinal anesthetic for elective knee arthroscopy. Two days later she develops a frontal and occipital headache that is much worse when she sits up and improves when she lies flat. She also reports tinnitus and intermittent diplopia. She is afebrile, her back is not tender, and her neurological examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Spinal anesthesia injects local anesthetic into the subarachnoid space after penetrating the dura and arachnoid, and post-spinal headache from CSF leak is a listed complication. The classic presentation of post-dural puncture headache is onset 6 hours to 3 days after dural puncture, a postural component that is worse when sitting, occipital or frontal localization, and possible tinnitus and diplopia, which is exactly this presentation.

optionExplanations.b: A subarachnoid hematoma is a listed complication but would be expected to produce neurological deficits rather than a purely postural headache.
optionExplanations.c: An epidural hematoma is also listed as a complication of neuraxial blockade but presents with neurological findings, not a postural headache with tinnitus.
optionExplanations.d: Infection is a recognized complication of neuraxial techniques, but she is afebrile with no local findings.
optionExplanations.e: Spinal cord trauma is avoided by inserting the needle below L2 and would cause deficits rather than a postural headache.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman is receiving bupivacaine for a peripheral nerve block before forearm surgery. Partway through the injection she reports numbness of the tongue, a metallic taste and tinnitus, then becomes drowsy and has a generalized convulsion. Help has been called, 100% oxygen is given, her ABCs are managed, and an anticonvulsant has been administered. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional treatment?
questions.explanation: Local anesthetic systemic toxicity occurs with accidental intravascular injection, local anesthetic overdose, or unexpectedly rapid absorption. CNS effects appear in order as numbness of the tongue, perioral tingling and metallic taste, disorientation and drowsiness, tinnitus, visual disturbances, muscle twitching, unconsciousness and convulsions. Treatment is early recognition and getting help, 100% oxygen and management of ABCs, diazepam or another anticonvulsant, management of arrhythmias, and Intralipid 20% to bind local anesthetic in the circulation.

optionExplanations.b: Dantrolene treats the hypermetabolic crisis of malignant hyperthermia, not local anesthetic toxicity.
optionExplanations.c: Naloxone reverses opioid overdose, and no opioid has been implicated in this reaction.
optionExplanations.d: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and would remove the anticonvulsant cover in a patient who is seizing.
optionExplanations.e: Sodium bicarbonate does not bind circulating local anesthetic; arrhythmias are managed on their own merits.

questions.question: A 71-year-old woman rates her pain as 3 out of 10 on the day after a minor day-surgery procedure. She has asthma, chronic renal insufficiency and a history of gastric ulceration. She has normal liver function and no allergies, and she is tolerating oral intake. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial analgesic?
questions.explanation: Pharmacological treatment of acute pain is guided by the WHO analgesia ladder, which begins with a non-opioid for mild pain. Acetaminophen is first-line for mild acute pain, is opioid-sparing, and is limited by an analgesic ceiling with a maximum dose of 4 g/24 h. NSAIDs are used with caution in patients with asthma, coagulopathy, GI ulcers, renal insufficiency and third-trimester pregnancy, and this patient has three of those cautions.

optionExplanations.b: Ibuprofen is an NSAID, and NSAIDs are cautioned in asthma, GI ulcers and renal insufficiency.
optionExplanations.c: Naproxen carries the same NSAID cautions and can reduce renal perfusion and cause gastric ulceration or bleeding.
optionExplanations.d: Ketorolac is an intravenous NSAID and shares the same cautions; her pain is mild and she tolerates oral intake.
optionExplanations.e: Oral opioids are indicated for moderate acute pain and parenteral opioids for moderate to severe pain, which is a step above this patient's mild pain.

source.reference: A25 — Pharmacological Management of Acute Pain

questions.question: A 54-year-old man is undergoing an elective open hemicolectomy under general anesthesia maintained with sevoflurane. Before induction the anesthesiologist completes the preanesthetic checklist and attaches a pulse oximeter, blood pressure monitor, ECG, and capnography. According to the Canadian guidelines to the practice of anesthesia and patient monitoring, which additional monitor must be used continuously for this case?
questions.explanation: The routine monitors for all cases are a pulse oximeter, BP monitor, ECG, capnography, and an agent-specific anesthetic gas monitor when inhalational anesthetic agents are used. Because maintenance is with sevoflurane, the agent-specific gas monitor is required in addition to the monitors already applied. A temperature probe, peripheral nerve stimulator, stethoscope, spirometry, and a manometer to measure ETT cuff pressure must also be available, but availability is not the same as continuous routine monitoring.

optionExplanations.b: End-tidal inhaled anesthetic monitoring and EEG monitoring such as a Bispectral Index monitor can be used as assessments of anesthetic depth, but they are optional rather than routine monitors for all cases.
optionExplanations.c: Central venous pressure is one of the hemodynamic elements that may be monitored in selected patients; it is invasive and is not part of routine monitoring for all cases.
optionExplanations.d: Pulmonary artery pressure and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure monitoring are reserved for selected patients and are not routine monitors.
optionExplanations.e: A peripheral nerve stimulator must be available, along with a temperature probe and stethoscope, but it is not one of the continuous monitors required for all cases.

source.reference: A7 — Monitoring: Routine Monitors for All Cases

questions.question: A 62-year-old man undergoing an elective open nephrectomy has lost approximately 600 mL of blood. He is mildly tachycardic, his hemoglobin remains well above the transfusion trigger, and the surgeon expects little further bleeding. The anesthesiologist decides to maintain euvolemia with crystalloid rather than a colloid or blood product. Which is the most appropriate fluid regimen?
questions.explanation: To maintain euvolemia in a patient with blood loss, 3 mL of crystalloid is infused per 1 mL of blood loss (3:1 replacement), so 600 mL of blood loss calls for roughly 1800 mL. Consensus guidelines recommend a balanced crystalloid such as Ringer's lactate over normal saline for routine replacement and resuscitation, because too much NS may lead to hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis.

optionExplanations.a: A 1:1 infusion-to-blood-loss ratio applies to colloid, which distributes within the intravascular volume; crystalloid distributes throughout the ECF and requires 3:1 replacement.
optionExplanations.b: This choice is wrong on both counts: 1:1 replacement applies to colloid, and a balanced crystalloid is preferred over normal saline.
optionExplanations.d: The volume is correct, but if large volumes are to be given, balanced fluids such as Ringer's lactate or Plasmalyte are preferred, as too much NS may lead to hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis.
optionExplanations.e: D5W contains no sodium, and it is the salt-containing crystalloids that distribute within and expand the ECF; it is not used to replace surgical blood loss.

questions.topic: IV Fluids and Blood Loss Replacement

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman is in the post-anesthetic care unit 30 minutes after an elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy under general anesthesia. She is a non-smoker with a history of motion sickness and received perioperative opioids. She now feels nauseated and vomits once. She is alert with a patent airway and rates her pain as 2 out of 10. Which is the most appropriate next step in her assessment?

options.text: Measure her blood pressure and heart rate
Assess for residual paralysis from the anesthetic

questions.explanation: Nausea and vomiting is a common postoperative anesthetic complication, and hypotension and bradycardia must be ruled out before the symptoms are attributed to the anesthetic, or to pain and surgical manipulation. Her young age, female sex, non-smoking status, history of motion sickness, and use of perioperative opioids are all recognized risk factors for PONV. Once a hemodynamic cause is excluded, treatment is with an antiemetic such as dimenhydrinate or ondansetron.

optionExplanations.b: Hypoglycemia is a metabolic disturbance considered in the workup of postoperative confusion and agitation, not the first thing to exclude in postoperative nausea and vomiting.
optionExplanations.c: Hyponatremia, especially post-TURP, is likewise part of the assessment of postoperative confusion and agitation rather than of isolated nausea and vomiting.
optionExplanations.d: Residual paralysis from the anesthetic is looked for when assessing postoperative confusion, agitation, or inadequate ventilation; she is alert with a patent airway.
optionExplanations.e: Hypotension and bradycardia are detected with routine vital signs; nothing in her presentation points to an arrhythmia requiring a 12-lead ECG first.

source.reference: A24 — Postoperative Care: Common Postoperative Anesthetic Complications

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman at 38 weeks gestation is positioned supine on the operating table before an elective caesarean section. Within two minutes she becomes pale, lightheaded, and nauseated, and her blood pressure falls from 118/70 to 82/44 mmHg. The fetal heart rate tracing shows a deceleration. Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Place a wedge under her right flank to produce approximately 15 degrees of left uterine displacement
Place a wedge under her left flank to tilt her toward the right

questions.explanation: A pregnant patient is prone to decreased BP due to aortocaval compression, the supine hypotensive syndrome, which is compounded by the physiologic decrease in SVR of pregnancy. The corrective manoeuvre is to position her in left uterine displacement of approximately 15 degrees using a wedge under the right flank when supine, which relieves the compression and restores venous return.

optionExplanations.b: A wedge under the left flank tilts her to the right and worsens aortocaval compression; the gravid uterus must be displaced to the left.
optionExplanations.c: Trendelenburg does not displace the uterus off the great vessels, and head-down positioning further limits respiratory excursion in a patient who already has a decreased FRC and increased O2 consumption.
optionExplanations.d: Reverse Trendelenburg does not relieve aortocaval compression and may further reduce venous return and blood pressure.
optionExplanations.e: Sitting upright leaves the gravid uterus compressing the great vessels and does not correct the supine hypotensive syndrome.

source.reference: A27 — Obstetrical Anesthesia: Anesthesia Considerations in Pregnancy

questions.question: A 74-year-old man develops hypotension 10 minutes after a high spinal anesthetic for elective lower limb surgery. Mean arterial pressure is 54 mmHg and heart rate is 48 bpm. His skin is warm, with no peripheral vasoconstriction. Neck veins are flat and the JVP is not elevated. He is afebrile, and surgical blood loss has been minimal. Which type of shock best explains his hypotension?
questions.explanation: Spinal/neurogenic shock is described as hypotension from decreased sympathetic tone, occurring without tachycardia or peripheral vasoconstriction (warm skin), and a high spinal anesthetic interfering with sympathetic outflow is listed among the causes of intraoperative hypotension. High spinal/epidural anesthesia is also listed as a cause of sinus bradycardia, matching this man's heart rate of 48 bpm. Warm skin, flat neck veins, and hypotension without tachycardia immediately after a high spinal therefore point to loss of sympathetic tone rather than another mechanism.

optionExplanations.a: Hypovolemic/hemorrhagic shock is the most common form of shock but is due to a decrease in intravascular volume; blood loss here has been minimal and there is no tachycardia or peripheral vasoconstriction.
optionExplanations.c: Obstructive shock (e.g. tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, pulmonary embolism) gives increased JVP with distended neck veins and increased SVR, not flat neck veins and warm skin.
optionExplanations.d: Cardiogenic shock from myocardial dysfunction, dysrhythmia, ischemia, or acute valvular dysfunction also produces increased JVP, distended neck veins, and increased SVR with decreased cardiac output.
optionExplanations.e: Septic shock would be suggested by febrile illness or infection; he is afebrile and the hypotension began with the block.

source.reference: A13 — Blood Pressure: Causes of Intraoperative Hypotension/Shock

questions.question: A 64-year-old man is intubated for an elective laparotomy. The endotracheal tube is secured at the 26 cm mark at the right corner of his mouth. Oxygen saturation falls to 88%, and breath sounds are absent over the left chest but easily heard on the right. Capnography shows a normal end-tidal CO2 waveform, there is no abdominal distention, and chest excursion is unilateral. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: Right endobronchial intubation from a tube that is too deep
Accidental extubation from a tube that is too shallow
Obstruction of the endotracheal tube by secretions

questions.explanation: The source states that a malpositioned ETT that is too deep may result in right endobronchial intubation, which is associated with desaturation and left-sided atelectasis, and that the tip should lie at the midpoint of the trachea at least 2 cm above the carina, approximately the 20-23 cm mark at the right corner of the mouth for men. A normal ETCO2 waveform on capnography, the gold standard for confirming the ETT is in the airway, places the tube in the airway rather than the esophagus. A tube at 26 cm with desaturation and breath sounds only on the right therefore indicates it has been advanced past the carina into the right mainstem bronchus.

optionExplanations.b: Esophageal intubation is suspected when ETCO2 is zero or near zero on the capnograph, with breath sounds over the epigastrium and distention of the stomach; here the waveform is normal and there is no abdominal distention.
optionExplanations.c: Pneumothorax is on the DOPE differential for poor bilateral breath sounds, but the source links right endobronchial intubation with a right-sided tension pneumothorax, and the excessive 26 cm tube depth already explains the absent left-sided sounds.
optionExplanations.d: The source attributes accidental extubation, vocal cord trauma, and laryngeal paralysis to a tube that is too shallow; this tube sits deeper than the 20-23 cm range for men and is still ventilating one lung.
optionExplanations.e: Obstruction is also on the DOPE differential, but it would impair chest excursion and gas flow bilaterally rather than abolish breath sounds only over the left chest.

source.reference: A9 — Tube Insertion / Confirmation of Tracheal Placement of Endotracheal Tube
